speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) of the countries or cities that have recently started relaxing their lockdown or stay at home measures, which ones are Singapore monitoring closely and modelling ourselves after; and (b) what are the lessons that we are learning from them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Members will recall that we implemented the circuit breaker from 7 April, just two months ago.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am sure to some, it feels like two years ago.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At that time, the number of COVID-19 cases was rising rapidly, with community cases averaging more than 30 a day, compared to just a handful in early March.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is coupled with an outbreak in the migrant workers' dormitories in early April.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The circuit breaker imposed strict safe distancing measures, keeping people at home and only allowing basic essential services to continue.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The number of community cases then began to decline and we extended the circuit breaker to 1 June in order to slow the infection further.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We understand the impact that the measures have had on people’s lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: No one went out except for essentials and work.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We introduced measures to help Singaporeans cope with the circuit breaker but it was nonetheless a challenging two months.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Overall, the circuit breaker was painful but necessary to slow the transmission in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Eventually, the daily number of community cases came down to low single digits towards the end of the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the number of cases in the dormitories remained high, as pointed out by Mr Murali Pillai, it was partly due to proactive screening as part of our plan to clear the dormitories and prepare the workers to return to work.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The situation in the dormitories had come under control.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The time had come to begin our journey to resume activities, gradually and cautiously.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, we must be mindful that there are still infections in dormitories, and there are still undetected cases in the community as evidenced from the unlinked cases we discover from time to time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The global situation has also not fully stabilised.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some countries are seeing a second wave of infection, after reopening their economy and allowing social activities, as pointed out by Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we must remain vigilant even as we exit the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Christopher de Souza asked what we can learn from other countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Multi-Ministry Task Force has been monitoring the global situation and learning from the experiences of other jurisdictions, including their strategies for opening the economy and the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, New Zealand had moved from Alert Level 4, which is their highest alert level, to Level 3 on 28 April, and subsequently transitioned to Level 2 about two weeks later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In making these moves, the authorities took into account factors such as the number of daily cases to ensure the situation is under control, healthcare capacity to ensure the system can cope with potential rise in new cases once the restrictions are relaxed and adequacy of safety measures to prevent transmission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the situation differs for different jurisdictions, most have taken a cautious and risk-based approach in lifting restrictions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While workplaces have reopened, many authorities have retained measures to limit social interactions and restrict mixing of households in the early stages of opening, as these are known sources of transmission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Hong Kong, for example, limited social gatherings to eight persons and this has just been extended by two more weeks because of a new cluster.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The United Kingdom and Germany limited social gatherings to two persons.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore has decided to maintain tight restrictions on social gatherings and household visits in Phase One, except for visits to parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will allow gatherings of up to five persons in Phase Two initially and possibly relaxing this further if the situation remains under control.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many countries have also continued with basic preventive measures to reduce the risk of transmission in public places and workplaces and we must do the same.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These include safe distancing measures and wearing of masks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Taiwan has made mask-wearing mandatory on public transport and we have done so too.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: New Zealand allows businesses to operate subject to implementation of measures like maintaining safe separation between patrons, keeping contact tracing registers and regularly disinfecting shared surfaces.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Likewise, we require workplace premises that are permitted to open to put in place safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Digital solutions have been used in many countries as well, such as Australia, China, Israel and South Korea to support the gradual resumption of activities by enabling faster contact tracing and identification of clusters.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At work premises, workers should also avoid social interactions with colleagues, including meal times and break times.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One of the areas that has a high risk of transmission is at the pantry area where most workers, while taking a break, are likely to let their guard down.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, they remove their masks in order to enjoy a cup of coffee.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, that area is an area of high risk of transmission and we would like to remind everyone to exercise extra caution when you are at the pantry area and enjoying your break times.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also worked with the dormitory operators to strengthen management practices, so that workers can live safely in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These include tighter control of entry and exit, measures to limit inter-mixing of residents between blocks and levels, and staggered use of common facilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even then, it would initially only be for the purpose of work, and with tight arrangements to transport them to and from work.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also strengthen health surveillance by conducting regular testing of the residents and having them report their health conditions daily.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Any residents that test positive and their close contacts will be isolated expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the number of cases we detect among the migrant worker population may remain high for some time, some of them may be past infections and are not active cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Schools, student care centres and pre-schools will also reopen progressively, with precautionary measures in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, social gatherings are still not allowed, and everyone should only leave home for essential activities and should continue wearing a mask when doing so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Multi-Ministry Task Force will closely monitor Phase One.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If the community transmission rates remain low and stable, and the dormitory situation continues to be under control, we can move to Phase Two.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In Phase Two, a broader range of activities will resume and we expect most of the economy to be able to reopen.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also gradually re-open our borders for Singaporeans to conduct essential activities overseas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will share more details later, nearer the date.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, to ensure that we do not undo the efforts of the circuit breaker period, we will continue to adopt a more cautious approach for higher risk activities, such as those involving large numbers of people interacting with one another in enclosed spaces for prolonged periods of time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These include religious services, cultural venues such as arts performances, cinemas, museums and libraries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Nightclubs and bars, karaoke outlets and other public entertainment establishments have similar risk factors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Overseas and local experience has indicated that these settings can seed large clusters of transmission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At least 255 cases were linked to a nightclub cluster in South Korea’s Itaewon entertainment district in early May.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In Singapore, the Hero’s Bar cluster is another example.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Organisers of these activities and business owners would need to convince relevant agencies that they have robust plans to ensure safety, before we let them open.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We understand the anxiety that our people are facing and are acutely aware of the economic and social impact of prolonged closure of various sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All of us want to get back to normal as soon as possible, as quickly as possible, and to be able to see our friends and family members whom we have not seen for some time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, if we resume too many activities too quickly, there is a real risk of a resurgence in the number of COVID-19 cases or clusters, which may require us to re-impose strict measures and slow down the pace of resumption.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As restrictions are eased and more activities resume, it becomes even more critical that each of us exercise strong social responsibility to ensure that community transmission remains low.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need everyone to play their part: wear a mask when outside your home, maintain good personal hygiene and observe safe opening measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our combined efforts will help smoothen our journey of safe transition, and together, we can keep Singapore COVID-safe.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In relation to the proactive checking of the migrant workers that he mentioned, how long will it take to complete the checking of the migrant workers in the dormitories?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And if the time it takes is long or goes over to the expected time of start of Phase Two or Phase Three, how would it impact the timelines for Phase Two or Phase Three of the reopening of the economy?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But as we do so, when the workers have been cleared through this process, they will then be able to start work.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But I have spoken to various F&B outlets and basically, they are a bit worried and concern whether they are able to sustain the prolong closure of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, some of them say, "If you continue like this, we won't be able to open even when you say go ahead and open", because by then they would be insolvent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am not asking for nightclubs and bars to be opened because there is where the crowd is, but for some of the F&B outlets to be able to sit a few of the diners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Perhaps, we can look at the examples of Hong Kong, UK and New Zealand and see whether we are able to relax some of our measures, just like they have done.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We discussed this at length within the Multi-Ministerial Task Force on how we can open safely.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are a lot of requests from different economic sectors and social sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are fully mindful that any prolonged closure of the businesses will have a severe impact.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And today, many of the F&B outlets are allowed to do takeaways so they have some ability to sustain a basic level of business activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I know that is not enough because they do want to bring back their customers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And there are also F&B outlets that cannot do delivery and so on; it is not economical for them to do so, and therefore they really do want to bring back customers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we need to remember that opening F&B is not just allowing the workers to work.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It also means that you must allow the customers to go there and eat and dine in.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When you allow that, that means you must allow gatherings.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And if you allow gathering in the F&B, you must also allow gatherings outside because then it does not make sense to only allow the gatherings in the F&B.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even in Phase Two, we need to look at what are the settings that we will allow earlier opening.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I have mentioned, some of the dining in will probably be earlier, with some safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of the venues, for example, even religious organisations, we are in discussions with them, we want to engage them to discuss with them what are the safeguards that can be put in place so that they can also open early.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we also understand that because these involve a large number of people in a congregation, and therefore, additional safeguards have to be put in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I know everybody wants to be in Phase One, but I need to explain that Phase One is a safe opening phase, which means that it is likely to be very restrictive and we are not prepared to open it up too early, too quickly because that, in fact, may result in more cases emerging and in turn, will require us to re-impose some of the measures and as a result, may differ and slowdown Phase Two.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we prefer to keep Phase One safe so that we can open Phase Two safely, and hopefully faster, rather than to delay further because there are cases that will emerge.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we open too quickly, the community is not ready, the businesses are not ready, then you will allow infections to seep in and you have to re-introduce some of the measures and as a result, in fact, you will in turn slow down the opening process.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That means we want to make haste but less speed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is better for us to take a more cautious approach.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We fully understand the challenges faced by businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have measures to put in place and we do all we can to make sure that we do not delay the opening so long as we are able to ensure safety.
